chapter: Youth, the road and arrival in California
title: Early bass influences and refusing to slap the bass
summary: He names Ellington, Claude Hopkins, Don Redman and the Santo Domingans as inspirations, and says he lost jobs rather than slap the bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well, to cover these things so we get the early parts taken care of, is there anything in Atlantic City that we haven't covered?

Well, there may not be anything in Atlantic City, because Atlantic City was a small place. But I was thinking to some of the things that inspired, when I was in school some of the things I used to listen to. Naturally, Duke Ellington was first. But there was Claude Hopkins and Don Redman, and there was another band around New York called the Santo Domingans, and that was made up mostly of Cubans and guys from Barbados and Latin Americans, but you know, they played good swing music.

But Claude Hopkins... Wellman Braud was the first bass player I became conscious of. And Claude Hopkins had a bass player, I don't know his name to this day, but I'm sure I borrowed something from him. He used to play high on the neck of the bass, you know, and during this time very few guys could do that -- because they were stuck in the first two or three positions. During this period, there was a lot of guys who could make sounds on the bass, but they knew

nothing about harmony. They'd slap the bass. I remember losing a few jobs because I refused to slap the bass, because in the first place it hurts your hands, and in the next place there was nothing musical about it. And I've always been interested in sounds.

Yeah, I want to jump ahead, because I was thinking when I was in school I really didn't start out to be a Jazz musician at all. My thing was I wanted to be a Classical player until...not really a Classical player, but I never did think I would be able to learn to play like guys in Duke Ellington's band could play, you know -- because I knew that was impossible. Then after studying for a while, I saw, you know, the possibilities. When I learned about harmony, I could see how it wasn't so hard at all.
